thread.title: Weekly Market Preview: Trade Tensions, Q2 Earnings On Tap, Bank Stress Tests

author: Richard Saintvilus
title: Weekly Market Preview: Trade Tensions, Q2 Earnings On Tap, Bank Stress Tests
text:
Shutterstock photo "There’s nothing to see here…”
The phrase above is seemingly the attitude investors have taken when it comes to international trade rhetoric being spewed among the world’s two largest economies in U.S. and China. But mounting trade tensions involving the European Union (EU), which on Friday said it would begin implementing tariffs on $3.2 billion in U.S. imports, could add an extra layer of investment risk. This comes in retaliation to U.S tariffs imposed on EU steel and aluminum earlier this month.
Those concerns aside, equities still ended Friday’s trading session higher, thanks in large part for what continues to be better-than-expected earnings from market titans FedEx ( FDX ), Oracle ( ORCL ) and Micron ( MU ). Beyond the positive earnings, investors cheered OPEC’s (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) decision to increase oil production to around 600,000 barrels per day, which is significantly lower than the aggressive figure analysts feared would have impeded the oil rally.
This news helped the Dow Jones Industrial Average to end an eight-day skid, closing Friday up 119.19 points, or 0.5%, to 24,580.89. The S&P 500 gained 5.12 points to 2,754.88, up of 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite Index shed 0.26% to 7,692.82. Large-cap tech stocks Facebook ( FB ), Amazon ( AMZN ) and Netflix ( NFLX ) each this past week hit all-time highs. As the second quarter earnings spree gets under way in a couple of weeks, investors will look to see the extent to which these stocks, including their FAANG counterparts Apple ( AAPL ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) can continue to hit new records.
In that vein, given that we’ve already received earnings results from nine S&P 500 companies (with fiscal quarters ending in May), it’s safe to day that the earnings reporting cycle for the second quarter has gotten underway. There’s the prevailing question of whether we have reached a peak in earnings growth? Last month Michael Wilson, chief U.S. equity strategist and CIO of Morgan Stanley, said "[W]e think the market is digesting the fact that the tax cut last year has created a lower quality increase in US earnings growth that almost guarantees a peak rate of change by 3Q.”
As the Q2 earnings season approaches, investors must reconcile whether the so-called peak earnings argument is a justifiable reason to sell stocks, particularly those with strong and sustaining fundamentals. What’s more, stocks that are trading at cheap valuations (below the S&P 500’s P/E of 18) and offer good-to-great dividend yields (above the S&P 500’s 2.00%) should remain in high demand, especially if their earnings growth (though they be slower) continue to trend higher.
This topic is now even more relevant to bank stocks, which will be put to test this week - literally. Last week all of the major banks tested by the Federal Reserve met the regulatory minimums for capital, meaning they won’t need a bailout should another major recession comes.
“Despite a tough scenario and other factors that affected this year’s test, the capital levels of the firms after the hypothetical severe global recession are higher than the actual capital levels of large banks in the years leading up to the most recent recession,” said Randal Quarles, Fed Vice Chairman for Supervision.
This poking and prodding, however, was merely the first round of the annual physical banks must go through. The full result of the Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review — better known as CCAR — will be announced on June 28. At which point, investors in Bank of America ( BAC ), JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Citigroup ( C ) and Wells Fargo ( WFC ) will know whether their investments will yield higher dividends or approved for buybacks or both.
